Author: @DaxDoesDigital
Content:
I installed iOS 26 on my iPhone 13 Pro Max.... I love it! 💕 It's made my 4 year old phone look NEW again, and almost futuristic. It has a nice contemporary feel to it. I like how NOW on the lockscreen when charging it will give me a percetage, as well as how long it will take to get to the percentage you have set for it to stop at, if not 100%,  right there on the screen.....

...and toggling things on/off in settings ...those buttons have been upgraded too. New modern look. It's the attention to detail that's amazing. I'll be finding new things for weeks, which adds to that "new phone" feel I mentioned earlier. I didn't want to upgrade my phone!

I know it will be polarizing, but I love the Liquid Glass aesthetic! However, for those that have trouble with seeing the text and such, there are buttons for reducing the transparency as well as changing the contrast....

If you just don't like it at all, you can use the classic view/icons. Or change their color! Make them dark, tinted.... There's a BUNCH of new customizations Marques didn't even mention....

Plus a lot of upgraded functionality... Even the battery App - LOL 🤣 ..........This is crazy good! ...And YES - This is a divergence. Google has been working on the flat aesthetic. Apple and Android are going in difference directions now. I don't think there will be much copying going on like Marques was hinting at....

I hope the divergence continues, and I am definitely on the Apple/iPhone side here. I just love the Liquid Glass, clean aesthetic........

Author: @jesusiscomingsoon5665
Content:
Summary of Feature Requests for iOS 26 As a frequent user particularly while driving professionally I’d like to suggest the following improvements to enhance both usability and safety on iOS devices:
	1.	Disable Lock Screen Camera Shortcut
Please provide an option to turn off the swipe to open camera on the lock screen. It often opens unintentionally when I’m trying to view notifications, which is frustrating for users who don’t rely on that shortcut.
	2.	Accidental Touch Protection
There’s a recurring issue with unintentional screen interactions such as accidental calls or app launches especially when the phone is in a pocket or during Bluetooth calls while driving. A feature to prevent unintended touches, similar to Samsung’s “Accidental Touch Protection,” would be a valuable addition.
	3.	Keep Maps App Active During Phone Calls
While navigating with Maps, the app exits whenever I receive or make a call, creating a safety concern as I have to manually reopen it while driving. Allowing Maps to stay active during calls like some Android devices do would greatly improve the navigation experience and overall safety.

Author: @The.JZA.
Content:
4:18 If you go into Calendar settings in the Settings app, you can choose any calendar provider as your default. Once set, all new events—whether created manually, via Siri, or from features like the screenshot recognition—will be added to that calendar by default. This has been the case for quite a while.

You can also select text manually; if the system recognises it as an event, you’ll be given the option to create a calendar entry directly from it.

If you use multiple calendars (e.g. personal and work), it’s very easy to switch an event from one to another. Just open the event in the Calendar app, tap on “Calendar”, and select the desired calendar from your synced list. It’s quick and seamless.

This is one of the areas where I find iOS far superior to Android. Android often locks you into using Gmail and Google Calendar. If your work uses another provider, you’re out of luck—there’s usually no proper integration with Google Assistant, and cross-platform syncing (e.g. Google Calendar with Outlook) is often unreliable or unsupported.

On iPhone, I’ve got my personal and work calendars in one place, with full control over creating, moving, and managing events. It’s genuinely one of the most underrated features.

Author: @markanderson831
Content: I've said as much on 9to5, but, for me, the whole design aesthetic is flawed from the start. As an autistic individual, I struggle with complicated information and sensory situations, so the liquid glass design, while beautifully presented in the original presentation, is incredible difficult for me to use on a day to day basis. For me, there’s too much going on and where before I didn’t have to think about using floating controls, I now find myself pausing, staring at the controls and trying to separate the background layer from the glass layer as well as the icon layer, just to use a control. The accessibility lacking on the design is a massive step back for Apple, which has surprised and disappointed me. I don't want to have to "Reduce transparency" to use a design that others can use without modification.

Author: @evilAshTheDog
Content: The software development process at Apple is clearly broken... and I suspect I know why.  The "modern" way to create software is to have UI designers tackle the problem first.  They then give their designs to developers in the form of requirements to implement.  Once implemented, the testers are involved.  The process of going from "this doesn't work well" to "here's a better way" is incredibly slow and painful when software is developed like this.  The best software is written by ONE person with a vision - not a huge team with stories, backlogs, sprint reviews, blah blah blah.  Apps like the Photos app or the Camera app are not complicated - but they're made horrible by committee!  As for "Android has had this...", please remember that when writing software there are patents that often get in the way of copying a novel feature.  You can't just look at a feature and say, "Why doesn't Apple do this?  Android has done it for years!"  Do a patent search first.

Content: I'm really interested to try out that 3D effect on photos. I'll never forget when Daydream came out nearly ten years ago. None of the VR headsets have really captured that sense yet, but I can see this + the Vision Pro hinting at where this could be going. I know all the flaws it has, but still there's so much potential there for something really incredible.

Author: @justathought-17
Content:
There was a time when technology companies were genuinely centered around technological innovation—driven by engineering breakthroughs, not marketing strategies. Today, however, it feels as though many of these companies have deviated from that ethos, prioritizing aesthetics, brand narratives, and consumer manipulation over meaningful progress. The focus seems less on solving real problems or pushing boundaries, and more on sustaining consumer engagement through superficial enhancements.

Take smartphones, for instance. The annual release cycle has become more of a ritual than a necessity. We’re often presented with marginal upgrades—incremental camera tweaks, slightly faster processors, or minor design changes—heralded as revolutionary steps forward. In reality, these iterations rarely introduce anything fundamentally transformative. Devices should be launched not according to a fiscal calendar, but when they embody significant technological advancement.

The same applies to software. The modern trend of rebranding cosmetic updates—like new color palettes or user interface animations—as major system overhauls is intellectually insulting to the informed user. It reflects a troubling shift from substance to spectacle, from genuine problem-solving to illusion-building.

In many ways, tech companies have become lifestyle curators rather than technology pioneers. Their core products increasingly serve as vehicles for ecosystem lock-in and market expansion rather than as tools for empowerment or exploration. It’s disheartening to witness the dilution of what once made technology so exciting: its ability to surprise us not with sleekness, but with substance.

True innovation should disrupt—not decorate.

- obviously it's simply less clear, readable, accessible: worse contrast and visibility of UI

Author: @kuramadvs
Content:
Liquid Glass looks amazing, but honestly, I still really appreciate Apple’s consistent design language across devices. I know a lot of Android users (and even some Apple users) love having the ability to customize every little detail, but when functionality shifts around too much, it stops feeling intuitive.

I really notice it when I use a friend’s phone — something as simple as pulling down Control Center can feel completely unfamiliar. A few years ago, if you had an iPhone, you basically knew how to use anyone else’s too. That consistency created a kind of muscle memory that’s starting to fade.

It reminds me of when my dad got the iPhone 4s on release. I told him to update, but he didn’t like the changes — mostly because he’d already dealt with the same thing on his iMacs and MacBooks. He had his own companies and relied on his devices to get work done efficiently. Aesthetics weren’t important to him — he just wanted things to stay functional and familiar. Of course, he’d still update when needed for compatibility or security, but from a functional standpoint, especially on his work devices, he wasn’t a fan of constant design and UI changes.

Back then I didn’t get it — now I kinda do.

Screenshots — I just want to take one with a single action. It should be quick and simple. If I need more options, I’ll tap the screenshot and do it there.

Author: @larswyness
Content:
We had a moment where the UI of Android diverged sharply away from iOS and it was around Ice Cream Sandwich. ICS introduced a LOT of elements that were unique and not seen many other places, like tabs you could swipe between, the hamburger menu (RIP) and the widget stacks on your lockscreen. 
Apps using Holo were truly a shift away from the chaotic Android look and feel, which didn't really have much consistency at all and shifted to unifying the look and feel so Android could get more consistency ala iOS. 

Apple would then move away from skeumorphism and follow in Android's footsteps for quite a few years, until google seemingly gave up (around Material 2) where they started changing things just to change them and actually started removing UI features. 

This divergence will likely draw some companies to try and implement liquid glass-esque design, but I sincerely hope they don't bother, because the amount of battery that will be used to render effects on common components that nobody's going to even notice 99% of the time, will be pointless. Material Expressive is a better idea, as the feel of elements jumping around is easily noticeable and relatively cheap to render.

Author: @sinoubrh
Content:
"Liquid Glass" for iOS – what a concept! For a company that champions accessibility and "human rights" in design, this new aesthetic is a head-scratcher.
Did anyone actually test this for readability? When text blurs into a translucent background, it doesn't look "fluid"; it looks illegible. The contrast issues are glaring, making your interface a nightmare for anyone with even minor vision impairments, or frankly, just trying to read in a bright room.
It seems they've prioritized a fleeting visual "wow" over fundamental usability. They've managed to make screens less functional in the pursuit of a specific style.
Frankly, it feels like a step backward for accessibility, forcing users to squint and struggle. Great job making our screens look perpetually smudged for the sake of "beauty."

Author: @rml695
Content: My favorite feature wasn’t mentioned at WWDC but revealed during GAAD, Global Accessibility Awareness Day: Accessible Reader. To see the benchmark if you go into Microsoft edge and then send yourself to any major website, look in the URL bar. You should see a picture of a book with some sound waves coming out of the upper right corner. That is the immersive reader. If you don’t see that, you can type read:// before the beginning of the URL and what that will do is that will basically reframe the entire webpage much like other web-based reading modes, except this one’s on steroids with natural sounding read aloud, speech, and a lot of of text customization. The accessibility reader takes this concept and makes it systemwide across all of Apple’s devices and apps. That’s honestly the number one thing I’m looking forward to this year. :-)

Author: @Proteus846
Content:
I’m very excited for the new versions of iOS and macOS (not enough to put the beta on the devices I need to be functional every day…) but as someone who uses my devices for functional purposes and not to show off I obviously am not a fan of “Liquid Glass.” It looks impressive, of course, but after years of ugly UI (since iOS 7) Apple finally got the look just right and their devices can only really improve visually in small ways at this point — and Liquid Glass is a huge step backward in every way except impressing the simple-minded and easily amused. Hopefully they’ll decrease the glassy effect more during future betas, or at least give a better option for a sensible design than the old “reduce transparency” accessibility feature.

Aside from making it look like I’m using my phone in the rain, the update features a lot of great changes. This is the first year I’m considering upgrading my iPhone 14 Pro Max to get Apple Intelligence (I have it on my M2 iPad Pro and what uses it has are more useful on a tablet than a phone) due to some actually-useful ML features. Hopefully the new iPhones aren’t as hideous as the leaks say, and US carriers have some good deals this time around.
